profile.reading:
This registry entry, listed under the name Delivery Emergency Response Center and attributed to the utility PSE&G, sits on Park Avenue in Bridgewater Township, Somerset County, New Jersey. PSE&G, formally Public Service Electric and Gas Company, is part of the PSEG family of companies and is New Jersey's largest electric and gas utility. Within PSE&G, Delivery is the business unit responsible for the physical distribution of electricity and natural gas to customers, as distinct from PSEG's separate power generation business.

An emergency response center, in utility terminology, is typically a coordination facility used to stage crews, dispatch trucks, and manage restoration efforts during storms, gas leaks, and other outage events, rather than a facility built to house servers or IT equipment for third party customers. PSE&G's own public materials describe extensive storm response and outage tracking infrastructure across its New Jersey service territory, consistent with that function, but do not name or describe a specific Bridgewater facility by this title.

No square footage, power capacity, tenancy, or construction history for this specific building is published by PSE&G, and none was found in available public records. Based on its name and its operator's line of business, this location reads as utility grid operations infrastructure rather than as a conventional data center, and it is presented here on that basis.

reading:
PSE&G, formally Public Service Electric and Gas Company, is the regulated New Jersey electric and gas utility owned by Public Service Enterprise Group and headquartered in Newark. It is the largest utility in the state, and it belongs in a data centre registry mainly as a supplier of electricity rather than as an operator of computing halls. Its published Data Center Solutions offering sells tailored high voltage service to data centre developers in New Jersey and in PSEG's Long Island and Rockaways service area, at 138 kV, 230 kV or 345 kV, and it asks for dedicated parcels of roughly 2.5 to 7 acres depending on the voltage chosen. That is utility service, the power a finished building will be able to draw from the grid. It is not an IT load, it is not standby generation, and it should never be reprinted as anyone's capacity.

The single facility this registry holds under the PSE&G name is not a data centre. It is a building on Park Avenue in Bridgewater Township, Somerset County, named in the source data as the PSE&G Delivery Emergency Response Center. Delivery is the PSE&G business unit responsible for the poles, wires and pipes that carry electricity and gas to customers, as distinct from PSEG's generation business. An emergency response centre, in utility usage, is where crews are staged and restoration work is dispatched during storms, gas leaks and outages, not where servers are racked for tenants.

The origin of the row is traceable in full. The building was drawn in OpenStreetMap on 17 August 2019 by a local mapper working from Bing aerial imagery, in a changeset whose own comment records that the mapper had added a new utility facility, with the words data center in brackets after it. The machine tag telecom equals data_center was present on the very first version of the object, and two further edits later that month added the building and operator tags while leaving that tag untouched. Any aggregator that harvests the tag inherits a data centre nobody ever verified, which is how facility counts inflate without anyone deciding to inflate them.

What is actually on the site is visible in the same data. The building stands about 106 metres from the Mountain Avenue Substation, a 69 kV distribution substation mapped at the same location, and a 69 kV line attributed to Public Service Enterprise Group runs nearby. New Jersey's statewide parcel composite places the building on parcel 1806_382_5.01, block 382 lot 5.01 in Bridgewater Township, a site of roughly 9.4 acres, and that layer publishes no owner name or improvement detail for it.

PSE&G publishes no square footage, power figure, tenancy or construction history for this building, and none was found in municipal or county records. Nothing in the public record supports calling it a data centre. It reads as grid operations infrastructure in a substation yard, and the row is kept so that the mistake stays visible rather than being quietly repeated.
